sec.s: Revision checklist

b.x: Relational algebra provides formal operations for manipulating relations. Selection, represented by σ, chooses rows that satisfy a condition. Projection, represented by π, chooses attributes or columns. Joins combine related rows from tables, allowing information to be retrieved across a relational schema. SQL implements these ideas through WHERE, SELECT, JOIN, and other query constructs, while adding practical features such as NULL, duplicate handling, and database-specific syntax.

SQL commands define structures and manipulate data. CREATE defines objects, ALTER changes structures, and DROP removes objects. INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes existing rows, and DELETE removes rows. SELECT retrieves data. WHERE filters rows, ORDER BY controls result ordering, and GROUP BY supports aggregation.

Nested queries allow one query to use another query's result. IN tests membership in a set, EXISTS tests whether a matching row exists, and correlated subqueries refer to the outer query. Views package a query under a name and can simplify access to data. Stored procedures are explicitly invoked routines supported by many database systems. Triggers execute automatically when configured database events occur. Their exact syntax and capabilities depend on the DBMS; SQLite does not provide server-style stored procedures in the same way as many server databases.

SQL injection occurs when untrusted input changes the structure or meaning of a SQL statement. The primary defense for ordinary database queries is to use parameterized queries or prepared statements, binding values separately from SQL text. Input validation, database constraints, safe error handling, least privilege, secure credential management, updates, monitoring, and tested backups add further layers of protection.

The most important practical habit is to separate code from data. Do not build SQL by concatenating untrusted values. Use the parameter-binding interface provided by the database driver. When dynamic table or column names are required, select them from a strict allowlist. Stored procedures can support security when designed correctly, but they are not automatically safe. Query safety, data integrity, authentication, and authorization are distinct concerns; a dependable application needs all of them.

sec.t: Complete Relational Algebra: Rename, Assignment, Division, Outer Joins, Aggregation
sec.s: The remaining operators of relational algebra, with worked examples and equivalence rules.

b.x: Earlier sections covered selection σ, projection π, joins ⋈, union, intersection, difference and the Cartesian product. A complete treatment of relational algebra needs a few more tools: rename (ρ), assignment (←), division (÷), outer joins, and the extended operators for computed columns and aggregation. This section adds these and then explains the algebraic equivalence rules that a query optimizer uses to rewrite queries.
24.1 Rename operator ρ

Relational algebra works on relations, and every result is itself a relation. Sometimes the attribute names of a result collide, or you need to join a relation with itself. Rename gives a relation or its attributes a new name.

x: ρ S (R)            rename relation R to S
ρ S(A1, A2, A3) (R) rename R to S and its attributes to A1, A2, A3
ρ (A1/B1, A2/B2) (R) rename attribute B1 to A1 and B2 to A2

b.x: The classic use is a self join. To find pairs of employees who work in the same department, we need two copies of EMPLOYEE:

x: π E1.name, E2.name ( σ E1.dept = E2.dept ∧ E1.eid < E2.eid ( ρ E1(EMPLOYEE) × ρ E2(EMPLOYEE) ) )

b.x: The condition E1.eid < E2.eid removes pairs of an employee with himself and also avoids listing each pair twice. In SQL the same idea is written with table aliases: FROM Employee E1, Employee E2.
24.2 Assignment operator ←
A long algebra expression becomes difficult to read. Assignment stores an intermediate result in a temporary relation variable, so the query can be written in steps.
Assignment does not add power to the language. It is notation that makes expressions easier to follow, just as a WITH clause (a common table expression) does in SQL.
24.3 Division operator ÷

Division answers questions that contain the words 'for all' or 'every'. Let R(A, B) and S(B) be relations, where the attributes of S are a subset of the attributes of R. Then R ÷ S contains every value a of A such that, for every tuple b in S, the pair (a, b) is present in R.

x: R ÷ S = π A (R) − π A ( ( π A (R) × S ) − R )

b.x: The formula shows that division is a derived operator. Read it in words: take all candidate A-values, build every pair they would need to have to qualify (candidates × S), subtract the pairs that actually exist in R, and what remains are the pairs that are missing. Any A-value that has a missing pair is disqualified. The A-values left over qualify.

b.h: Worked example: students who have completed ALL required courses

b.x: Meera is missing the pair (Meera, Python), so she is removed. Step by step: π student(COMPLETED) = {Aarav, Meera, Kabir}; the cross product with REQUIRED has 9 pairs; subtracting COMPLETED (8 rows) leaves only (Meera, Python); projecting on student gives {Meera}; the final subtraction gives {Aarav, Kabir}.
SQL has no division operator, so we translate it
The standard translation uses a double NOT EXISTS. Read it as: 'there is no required course for which this student has no completed record.'
A counting version is often shorter and faster. It counts how many required courses each student has and compares with the total number of required courses:

x: JOIN Required r ON r.course = c.course
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c.course) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Required);

Forgetting the JOIN to REQUIRED in the counting version. A student with five completed courses but only two of the required ones would otherwise be counted wrongly. Also remember that division is not defined when S is empty in the usual textbook sense: every candidate would qualify vacuously.

b.x: 24.4 Outer joins in algebra
The natural (inner) join drops tuples that have no partner. Outer joins keep them and fill the missing side with NULL.

x: All tuples of R are kept. Unmatched R tuples get NULLs for S's attributes.
All tuples of S are kept. Unmatched S tuples get NULLs for R's attributes.
All tuples of both are kept. The result is the left and right outer joins combined.

b.x: Outer joins are useful for questions such as 'list all students and the courses they take, including those who take none'. An outer join can be written as an inner join union the unmatched tuples padded with NULLs, so it is derived rather than fundamental, but it needs NULL as a value, which is why the pure relational model of Codd treats it as an extension.
24.5 Generalized projection and aggregation
Generalized projection allows arithmetic expressions and functions in the projection list:
The aggregate operator is written with the calligraphic G (or sometimes γ). Its form is: grouping attributes on the left of G, aggregate functions on the right.

x: dept G COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal (EMPLOYEE)
G SUM(amount) (PAYMENT)        (no grouping: one result row)
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal

b.x: Supported aggregate functions are SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX and COUNT. Grouping splits the relation into partitions that agree on the grouping attributes, then applies the functions once per partition.
24.6 Sets versus bags

Pure relational algebra uses set semantics: a relation never has duplicate tuples. SQL uses bag (multiset) semantics: duplicates are allowed unless you ask for DISTINCT. This is why SQL has both UNION (set) and UNION ALL (bag), and why SELECT without DISTINCT may return the same row several times. Projection in pure algebra removes duplicates automatically; SQL's SELECT does not because removing duplicates needs a sort or hash step that costs time.
24.7 Equivalence rules for optimization
Two algebra expressions are equivalent if they give the same result on every database. Optimizers use equivalences to find cheaper but identical plans.

x: Cascade of selections: σ c1 ∧ c2 (R) = σ c1 ( σ c2 (R) ).
Selections commute: σ c1 ( σ c2 (R) ) = σ c2 ( σ c1 (R) ).
Cascade of projections: π L1 ( π L2 (R) ) = π L1 (R) when L1 ⊆ L2.
Selection and projection commute when the selection uses only attributes kept by the projection: π L ( σ c (R) ) = σ c ( π L (R) ) if c uses only attributes in L.
Joins and products are commutative: R ⋈ S = S ⋈ R. Natural joins are also associative: (R ⋈ S) ⋈ T = R ⋈ (S ⋈ T).
Selection can be pushed through a join: if c uses only attributes of R, then σ c (R ⋈ S) = ( σ c (R) ) ⋈ S.
Selection distributes over union, and over difference when applied to both sides: σ c (R ∪ S) = σ c (R) ∪ σ c (S).
A selection combined with a Cartesian product equals a join: σ θ (R × S) = R ⋈ θ S.

'Push selections and projections down as far as possible' is the first heuristic of query optimization. Reducing the number of tuples before an expensive join is almost always a win, and rules 3, 4 and 6 are the justification.

sec.s: A declarative way to say what you want: tuple relational calculus, domain calculus and Codd's theorem.

b.x: Relational algebra is procedural: you describe a sequence of operations. Relational calculus is declarative: you describe the properties of the result without saying how to compute it. Calculus comes in two flavours, tuple relational calculus (TRC) whose variables range over tuples, and domain relational calculus (DRC) whose variables range over attribute values. SQL is strongly influenced by TRC.
25.1 Tuple relational calculus (TRC)
A TRC query has the form:
It means: the set of all tuples t for which the predicate P is true. Here t is a tuple variable. Atoms (basic conditions) are of three kinds:

x: R(t): t is a tuple of relation R.
t.A θ s.B: compares an attribute of t with an attribute of s, where θ is one of =, ≠, <, ≤, >, ≥.
t.A θ c: compares an attribute of t with a constant.

b.x: Formulas are built from atoms with the connectives ∧ (and), ∨ (or), ¬ (not), ⇒ (implies), and the quantifiers ∃ (there exists) and ∀ (for all). Remember that P ⇒ Q is equivalent to ¬P ∨ Q.
25.2 Free and bound variables

A variable is bound when it is introduced by a quantifier, as in ∃e. A variable that is not quantified is free. In { t | P(t) } the variable t is free, and it is the free variable that determines the shape of the result. Bound variables are only helpers, like the loop variable in a program.
25.3 Worked TRC queries
Query 1: students of the BCA department with CGPA above 8.
Query 2: names only (a projection). The result tuple is built from selected attributes of t:
Query 3: students enrolled in at least one course (an existential quantifier plays the role of a join):
Query 4: students who are enrolled in every course (a universal quantifier plays the role of division):

x: { s | STUDENT(s) ∧ ∀c ( COURSE(c) ⇒ ∃e ( ENROLMENT(e) ∧ e.sid = s.sid ∧ e.cid = c.cid ) ) }

b.x: Query 5: students who are not enrolled in any course (negation plays the role of difference):
25.4 Safe expressions
Some calculus expressions describe an infinite result. For example:

This is the set of all tuples that are not in STUDENT, which is infinite. A database system can never compute such an answer. An expression is called safe if every value in its result comes from the domain of the expression, that is, from the constants in the formula and the values that actually appear in the relations mentioned. Only safe expressions are accepted as queries. Safety also guarantees that the language is no more powerful than what can be computed on a finite database.

x: Writing a query with ¬ or ∨ and forgetting that every free variable must be tied to a relation by a positive atom such as STUDENT(s). Without that, the expression is unsafe.

b.x: 25.5 Domain relational calculus (DRC)
In DRC the variables stand for individual values, not for whole tuples. A query looks like:
The atom R(x1, ..., xn) is true when the tuple of values is in R. DRC is closer to the logic notation used in Prolog and Datalog, and the language Query-by-Example (QBE) is based on it.

x: { < n, d > | ∃ s, c ( STUDENT(s, n, d, c) ∧ c > 8 ) }
{ < n > | ∃ s, d, c ( STUDENT(s, n, d, c) ∧ d = 'BCA' ) }

b.x: The first query lists the name and department of students with CGPA above 8. Note that each position in the STUDENT atom is filled by a variable or constant, in the order of the attributes.
25.6 The same query in four languages
Query: names of students enrolled in the course 'DBMS'.

x: π name ( STUDENT ⋈ ENROLMENT ⋈ σ title='DBMS' (COURSE) )
JOIN Enrolment e ON e.sid = s.sid
JOIN Course c    ON c.cid = e.cid

b.x: (In the DRC line the underscore stands for 'any value', a credits value we do not care about.)
25.7 Codd's theorem and relational completeness

Codd's theorem states that relational algebra, safe tuple relational calculus and safe domain relational calculus are equivalent in expressive power. Every query that can be written in one can be written in the others. A query language is called relationally complete if it can express every query that relational algebra can express.

x: Algebra to calculus is easy: each operator has a direct logical meaning (σ is a condition, π drops variables, ⋈ is ∃ with an equality, difference is ¬).
Calculus to algebra is the harder direction and uses the safety condition to bound the values needed.

SQL is relationally complete, and in practice is more powerful than the pure languages because it adds aggregation, grouping, ordering, NULLs, arithmetic and recursive queries (which neither pure algebra nor pure calculus can express).

Remember the one-line summary: algebra says HOW (a sequence of operators), calculus says WHAT (a logical condition), and Codd proved they have the same power. TRC corresponds to SQL's style; DRC corresponds to QBE.

sec.s: Every join type with result tables, ON versus WHERE, semi and anti joins, and the NOT IN with NULL trap.

b.x: Joins combine rows from two or more tables. Section 5 explained the idea; this section shows the exact result of every join type, the traps that cause wrong answers, and the semi-join and anti-join patterns. All examples use these small tables.

Notice that Kabir and Isha have no enrolment, and the last enrolment row refers to sid 5, which does not exist in Student (this can happen if foreign keys are not enforced or after bad data loads). These two situations show the difference between join types.
26.1 INNER JOIN
Returns only the rows with a match on both sides.

x: FROM Student s INNER JOIN Enrolment e ON e.sid = s.sid;

b.x: 26.2 LEFT, RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN

x: -- LEFT JOIN: every Student row is kept
FROM Student s LEFT JOIN Enrolment e ON e.sid = s.sid;
-- RIGHT JOIN: every Enrolment row is kept
-- FULL OUTER JOIN: rows from both sides are kept (6 rows)
Aarav | DBMS    Aarav | C       Meera | DBMS
Kabir | NULL    Isha  | NULL    NULL  | Python

SQLite supports LEFT JOIN from the beginning but added RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN only in version 3.39. On an older SQLite (or an older Android system SQLite) swap the table order and use LEFT JOIN, and simulate FULL JOIN with a LEFT JOIN UNION ALL the unmatched rows of the other side. MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN and uses the same UNION trick.
-- FULL JOIN simulation that works everywhere
FROM Student s LEFT JOIN Enrolment e ON e.sid = s.sid
FROM Enrolment e LEFT JOIN Student s ON s.sid = e.sid

b.x: 26.3 CROSS JOIN

A cross join pairs every row of one table with every row of the other, giving m × n rows. With 4 students and 4 enrolments the result has 16 rows. It is useful for generating combinations (for example every student with every exam slot) but is usually a bug when it happens by accident, such as a join with a forgotten ON condition.

x: SELECT s.name, e.course FROM Student s CROSS JOIN Enrolment e;  -- 16 rows

b.x: 26.4 NATURAL JOIN and USING
NATURAL JOIN joins on all columns that have the same name in both tables and shows the common column once. USING (col) joins on an explicitly named common column.

x: SELECT name, course FROM Student NATURAL JOIN Enrolment;
SELECT name, course FROM Student JOIN Enrolment USING (sid);

NATURAL JOIN is risky in real projects. If someone later adds a column with the same name to both tables (for example created_at or name), the join condition silently changes and the results become wrong. Prefer an explicit ON or USING.

b.x: 26.5 Self join
A table joined to itself, using two aliases. A typical case is an employee table where each row stores the id of the employee's manager.

x: SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM Employee e LEFT JOIN Employee m ON m.eid = e.manager_id;

b.x: LEFT JOIN is used so that the top manager, who has no manager, still appears (with a NULL manager).
26.6 Non-equi joins
A join condition does not have to be an equality. Ranges and inequalities are common, for example mapping marks to grades:

x: FROM Marks m JOIN Grade g
ON m.score BETWEEN g.lo AND g.hi;

b.x: 26.7 ON versus WHERE in outer joins

For an INNER JOIN, a condition in ON and the same condition in WHERE give the same result. For an outer join they do not. ON decides which rows match; WHERE filters the rows after the join, including the NULL-extended rows.

x: -- Intention: all students, showing DBMS enrolments only
FROM Student s LEFT JOIN Enrolment e
-- Aarav DBMS, Meera DBMS, Kabir NULL, Isha NULL
-- With the condition in WHERE the NULL rows are removed
FROM Student s LEFT JOIN Enrolment e ON e.sid = s.sid
-- Aarav DBMS, Meera DBMS   (the LEFT JOIN acts like INNER JOIN)

b.x: 26.8 Semi-join and anti-join

A semi-join returns the rows of the left table that have at least one match in the right table, without repeating the left row for each match and without columns from the right table. SQL has no keyword for it; use EXISTS or IN.

x: -- Students who have at least one enrolment (semi-join)
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Enrolment e WHERE e.sid = s.sid);
-- Aarav, Meera (Aarav appears once even with two enrolments)

b.x: An anti-join returns the rows of the left table with no match. NOT EXISTS is the safe way.

x: WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Enrolment e WHERE e.sid = s.sid);
-- Also correct: LEFT JOIN and test for NULL
LEFT JOIN Enrolment e ON e.sid = s.sid

b.x: 26.9 The NOT IN and NULL trap
Suppose an enrolment row exists whose sid is NULL (unknown student). Then:

x: WHERE sid NOT IN (SELECT sid FROM Enrolment);

b.x: The reason is three-valued logic. NOT IN expands to sid <> 1 AND sid <> 1 AND sid <> 2 AND sid <> 5 AND sid <> NULL. The last comparison is UNKNOWN, so the whole AND can never be TRUE for any student. NOT EXISTS does not suffer from this problem because it asks 'is there a row', not 'is the value different from every value'.

x: If a question says 'find those who have not ...', the answer should use NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL. Mention the NOT IN with NULL problem to earn extra marks.

b.x: 26.10 Cardinality explosion

When you join a parent to two independent child tables, the rows multiply. Suppose Aarav has 2 enrolments and 3 fee payments. Joining Student to both Enrolment and Payment produces 2 × 3 = 6 rows for Aarav, so SUM(amount) is counted twice per payment and gives a wrong total.

x: Aggregate each child table in a subquery first, then join the summaries.
Or use COUNT(DISTINCT ...) carefully, remembering SUM(DISTINCT amount) is wrong when two different payments have the same amount.
Always check the number of rows after adding a join, especially with one-to-many relationships.

sec.t: Set Operations, CASE and NULL-Handling Functions
sec.s: UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT, CASE, COALESCE, NULLIF, three-valued logic and everyday SQLite functions.

b.x: 27.1 Set operations
Set operations combine the results of two SELECT statements vertically (rows are stacked), unlike joins, which combine tables horizontally (columns are added).

x: Rows that are in either result. Duplicates are removed.
Rows from both results, duplicates kept. Faster because no duplicate removal is needed.
Rows that appear in both results (duplicates removed).
Rows in the first result that are not in the second. Oracle calls this MINUS.

b.x: Rules for compatible queries: both SELECTs must return the same number of columns, the columns in the same positions must have compatible data types, and the column names of the final result are taken from the first query. ORDER BY may appear only once, at the very end, and refers to the column names of the first query.

x: -- Students of two classes: A_Class(name), B_Class(name)
SELECT name FROM B_Class;           -- each name once
SELECT name FROM B_Class;           -- in both classes
SELECT name FROM B_Class;           -- only in A

SQLite supports UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT and EXCEPT. Older MySQL versions did not have INTERSECT and EXCEPT; they were added in recent MySQL 8.0 releases. In the SQL standard INTERSECT binds more tightly than UNION and EXCEPT, but SQLite evaluates compound selects from left to right with equal priority, so use subqueries to make your intention explicit.
Using UNION when you mean UNION ALL. UNION silently removes real duplicates (two different students with the same name, two sales of the same amount) and costs an extra sort or hash step.

b.x: 27.2 CASE expressions
CASE is SQL's if-then-else and can appear in SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY and inside aggregate functions. There are two forms.

x: -- Searched CASE: conditions evaluated top to bottom
-- Simple CASE: compares one expression with values

b.x: The first WHEN that is true wins, so order the conditions from the most specific to the most general. If no WHEN matches and there is no ELSE, the result is NULL.
27.3 COALESCE, NULLIF and IFNULL

x: Returns the first argument that is not NULL. Standard SQL, accepts any number of arguments.
Two-argument version available in SQLite and MySQL. Oracle has NVL, SQL Server has ISNULL.
Returns NULL if a equals b, otherwise returns a.
-- Avoid division by zero: NULLIF turns 0 into NULL

b.x: Division by NULL returns NULL instead of raising an error (in SQLite division by zero already gives NULL, but in PostgreSQL it is an error, so the NULLIF habit is useful everywhere).
27.4 Three-valued logic

A comparison involving NULL is neither true nor false; it is UNKNOWN. SQL logic therefore has three truth values. WHERE keeps only the rows for which the condition is TRUE; both FALSE and UNKNOWN rows are discarded.

x: AND  | T  F  U         OR  | T  F  U        NOT
T   | T  F  U          T  | T  T  T        F -> T
F   | F  F  F          F  | T  F  U        U -> U
U   | U  F  U          U  | T  U  U
x IS NULL          -> TRUE or FALSE, never UNKNOWN
5 > NULL OR 1 = 1  -> TRUE (OR with a TRUE side is TRUE)

b.x: To compare two values and treat two NULLs as equal, use a null-safe comparison. PostgreSQL and the standard use a IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b; SQLite's IS and IS NOT operators work this way for ordinary values (a IS b is true when both are NULL), and newer SQLite versions also accept IS DISTINCT FROM; MySQL uses the operator <=>.
27.5 NULL in aggregates, grouping, sorting and constraints

x: Aggregate functions ignore NULLs: AVG(marks) divides by the number of non-NULL marks. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values.
If every value is NULL, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX return NULL, while COUNT returns 0. Use COALESCE(SUM(x), 0) when you need a zero.
GROUP BY puts all NULLs into one group, and DISTINCT treats NULLs as equal to each other, even though NULL = NULL is not true.

ORDER BY must place NULLs somewhere. SQLite and MySQL treat NULL as smaller than any value, so NULLs come first in ascending order. PostgreSQL and Oracle treat NULL as larger, so they come last. PostgreSQL and SQLite (recent versions) accept NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST to remove doubt.

A UNIQUE constraint treats each NULL as different, so most systems (SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle) allow several NULLs in a UNIQUE column. SQL Server is a well-known exception that allows only one.

b.x: 27.6 Pattern, range and list pitfalls

x: LIKE uses % (any number of characters) and _ (exactly one character). In SQLite, LIKE ignores case for ASCII letters by default; in PostgreSQL LIKE is case-sensitive and ILIKE is the case-insensitive form. SQLite also has GLOB, which is case-sensitive and uses * and ?.
To search for a literal percent sign use ESCAPE: WHERE note LIKE '50\%%' ESCAPE '\'.
BETWEEN a AND b includes both end values. For timestamps, WHERE d BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-01-31' misses rows on January 31 after midnight; use d >= '2026-01-01' AND d < '2026-02-01'.
x IN (1, 2, NULL) is TRUE when x is 1 or 2, but never FALSE (it becomes UNKNOWN); x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) is never TRUE.
A leading wildcard such as LIKE '%son' cannot use an ordinary index and forces a scan of the whole table.

b.x: 27.7 Everyday SQLite functions

x: Questions on NULL are a favourite. Be able to state: NULL is not a value but a marker for missing or unknown; any comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN; use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL; aggregates ignore NULL except COUNT(*); and NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns no rows.

sec.s: GROUP BY rules, conditional aggregation, ROLLUP, CUBE, GROUPING SETS, FILTER and string aggregation.

b.x: Section 10 introduced GROUP BY and the five aggregate functions. This section goes deeper: the rules that catch beginners, ways to compute several summaries in one pass, and the OLAP-style extensions ROLLUP, CUBE and GROUPING SETS used in reporting.
28.1 GROUP BY rules

x: GROUP BY divides the rows into groups that have identical values in the grouping columns; each group produces one output row.

In standard SQL every column in the SELECT list must either appear in GROUP BY or be inside an aggregate function. PostgreSQL and Oracle enforce this. SQLite and older MySQL are permissive and return an arbitrary row's value for a bare column, which hides bugs.
WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters whole groups after aggregation, so only HAVING may use aggregate functions.
You may group by an expression (GROUP BY strftime('%Y', d)) and in most systems by an output column alias or position number, though the standard does not require this.
WHERE product = 'Laptop'          -- row filter, before grouping
HAVING SUM(amount) > 450;         -- group filter, after grouping

Putting a condition on a plain column into HAVING when WHERE would do. WHERE is evaluated earlier and discards rows before the expensive grouping, so it is faster. Use HAVING only for conditions on aggregates.

b.x: 28.2 COUNT(*), COUNT(col) and COUNT(DISTINCT col)

x: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT course) FROM Enrolment;  -- 2 (DBMS, C)
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT sid)    FROM Enrolment;  -- 3 students

b.x: 28.3 Conditional aggregation (pivoting)

Putting CASE inside an aggregate lets you compute many different numbers in one scan of the table. This is also the standard way to turn rows into columns (a pivot) in databases without a PIVOT operator.

x: SUM(CASE WHEN product = 'Laptop' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS laptops,
SUM(CASE WHEN product = 'Phone'  THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS phones,

b.x: PostgreSQL and recent SQLite versions (3.30 and later) also support the standard FILTER clause, which says the same thing more clearly. MySQL does not have it, so use CASE there.
28.4 String aggregation

x: -- North | Laptop, Phone      South | Laptop, Phone

b.x: 28.5 ROLLUP, CUBE and GROUPING SETS

Reports often need detail rows, subtotals and a grand total together. Doing it with separate queries means scanning the table several times. These extensions of GROUP BY compute several groupings in one statement.
ROLLUP(region, product) produces groupings from the most detailed to the grand total, removing columns from the right: (region, product), (region), and ().

x: SELECT region, product, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM Sales GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, product);
-- MySQL 8: GROUP BY region, product WITH ROLLUP

b.x: CUBE(region, product) produces every possible combination of the columns: (region, product), (region), (product), (). The extra rows give product totals across regions: Laptop 900 and Phone 500. MySQL supports WITH ROLLUP but has no CUBE.
GROUPING SETS lets you list exactly the groupings you want, for example GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((region), (product), ()). ROLLUP and CUBE are shortcuts for particular sets.

The NULL in a subtotal row means 'all values', which is confusing if the column itself can contain NULL. The GROUPING(col) function returns 1 for a super-aggregate row and 0 for a normal row, so you can label rows with CASE WHEN GROUPING(region) = 1 THEN 'ALL' ELSE region END.
28.6 The SQLite workaround
SQLite has no ROLLUP, CUBE or GROUPING SETS. Use UNION ALL of the separate groupings; this gives the same rows (the order may differ, so add ORDER BY if needed).

x: SELECT region, product, SUM(amount) AS total FROM Sales
SELECT region, NULL, SUM(amount) FROM Sales GROUP BY region
SELECT NULL, NULL, SUM(amount) FROM Sales;
Remember the difference in the number of grouping sets: for n columns ROLLUP gives n + 1 sets, while CUBE gives 2 to the power n sets. For two columns that is 3 versus 4.

sec.s: Calculations across related rows without collapsing them: ranking, running totals, LAG and LEAD, frames.

b.x: An ordinary aggregate with GROUP BY collapses many rows into one. A window function performs a similar calculation over a set of related rows (the window) but keeps every row in the result. This makes it possible to compare each row with its group, rank rows, compute running totals and look at the previous row, all of which are awkward with plain SQL. Window functions are part of the SQL standard and are available in PostgreSQL, MySQL 8, Oracle, SQL Server and SQLite 3.25 or later.
29.1 Syntax

x: PARTITION BY col1, col2        -- optional: split rows into groups
ORDER BY col3 [ASC|DESC]       -- optional: order inside each group
frame_clause                   -- optional: which rows to include
PARTITION BY is like GROUP BY but does not collapse rows. Without it the whole result is one partition.
ORDER BY inside OVER orders the rows within the partition; it matters for ranking, LAG/LEAD and running totals.
The frame clause chooses a sliding set of rows around the current row.

b.x: 29.2 Aggregate versus window

x: -- Each employee together with the department average
AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS dept_avg

b.x: 29.3 Ranking functions
Three functions number the rows of a partition according to ORDER BY. They differ in how they treat ties.

x: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC, name) AS rn,
RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)       AS rnk,
DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)       AS drnk
Unique sequence 1, 2, 3 ... ties are broken arbitrarily unless ORDER BY is complete.
Ties share a rank and the next rank is skipped: 1, 1, 3, 4.
Ties share a rank and no number is skipped: 1, 1, 2, 3.
Splits the ordered rows into n nearly equal buckets numbered 1 to n (quartiles with n = 4).

b.x: 29.4 Top-N per group
A window function cannot be used directly in WHERE, because windows are computed after WHERE. Wrap the query in a subquery or a CTE and filter on the rank.

x: -- Two highest paid employees in every department
ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r

b.x: 29.5 LAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE

x: MonthlySales(month, amount): Jan 100, Feb 150, Mar 120, Apr 200
LAG(amount)  OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev,
LEAD(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS next,
amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change

b.x: LAG(col, n, default) looks n rows back (default 1) and returns the default instead of NULL when no such row exists. LEAD looks forward. FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE return the first or last value in the frame.

x: When ORDER BY is present and no frame is written, the default frame ends at the current row, so LAST_VALUE(x) returns the current row's own value. To get the last value of the whole partition write: LAST_VALUE(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING).

b.x: 29.6 Frames: ROWS and RANGE

A frame defines which rows around the current row take part in an aggregate window. The general form is ROWS (or RANGE) BETWEEN start AND end, where start and end are UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, n PRECEDING, CURRENT ROW, n FOLLOWING or UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. ROWS counts physical rows. RANGE works on values of the ORDER BY column and includes all peer rows with the same value.

x: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running,
ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2)   AS avg3,
ROUND(100.0 * amount / SUM(amount) OVER (), 1)     AS pct

b.x: The default frame, when ORDER BY is present, is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which is why SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY ...) gives a running total (with peer rows added together on ties). SUM(amount) OVER () with empty parentheses is the grand total, used above for percent of total.
29.7 Logical order of query evaluation

Understanding the order explains why you cannot use a column alias in WHERE or a window function in HAVING. The database processes a query conceptually in this order, although the physical plan may differ:

x: FROM and JOIN: build the working set of rows.
WHERE: remove rows that fail the condition.
Window functions: computed over the remaining rows.
SELECT: evaluate the output expressions and aliases.
ORDER BY: sort (aliases can be used here).
LIMIT / OFFSET: keep only the requested slice.

State the key difference clearly: GROUP BY returns one row per group, a window function returns one row per input row. If asked for 'rank of students within each department keeping all students listed', the answer is RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY marks DESC).

sec.t: Common Table Expressions and Recursive Queries
sec.s: WITH clauses, chained CTEs and recursive CTEs for hierarchies, series, graphs and bills of materials.

b.x: 30.1 What is a CTE?

A common table expression (CTE) is a named temporary result defined with the WITH keyword at the start of a statement. It exists only for that statement. You can think of it as a view that lives for one query. CTEs make long queries readable: instead of nesting subqueries inside subqueries, you name each step and use the names below.

x: -- emp(id, name, mgr, salary, dept) used in this section:
-- 1 Anil  NULL 90000 CSE   | 2 Bina 1 70000 CSE   | 3 Chetan 1 65000 ECE
-- 4 Divya 2    50000 CSE   | 5 Esha 2 50000 CSE   | 6 Farhan 3 45000 ECE
SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal FROM emp GROUP BY dept)
FROM emp e JOIN dept_avg d USING (dept)
WHERE e.salary > d.avg_sal ORDER BY e.name;

b.x: Several CTEs can be chained with commas, and a later CTE may use an earlier one: WITH a AS (...), b AS (SELECT ... FROM a) SELECT ... FROM b. Each CTE can be referenced several times in the main query, which avoids repeating the same subquery.
30.2 CTE versus subquery versus view

x: Anonymous, written in place, hard to read when nested deeply.
Named, defined once at the top, can be referenced more than once, can be recursive. Lives for one statement.
Stored in the catalog, reusable across statements and users, can carry privileges.
Physically stored for the session; can be indexed; useful when the intermediate result is large and reused.

b.x: 30.3 Recursive CTEs

A recursive CTE refers to itself. It has three parts: an anchor member (the starting rows), a recursive member (which joins the CTE with another table to produce the next layer of rows), and an implicit termination (the recursion stops when the recursive member returns no new rows). The two members are joined with UNION ALL (or UNION, which also removes duplicates and so can stop certain cycles).

x: recursive query referring to name   -- repeats until it returns nothing

b.x: 30.4 Example: walking an organisation chart

x: WITH RECURSIVE chain(id, name, lvl, path) AS (
SELECT id, name, 0, name FROM emp WHERE mgr IS NULL
SELECT e.id, e.name, c.lvl + 1, c.path || ' > ' || e.name
FROM emp e JOIN chain c ON e.mgr = c.id)
SELECT lvl, path FROM chain ORDER BY path;

b.x: The anchor selects the root (the employee with no manager). Each round of the recursive member finds the people whose manager was produced in the previous round: level 1 is Anil's reports, level 2 their reports, and so on. When a round finds nobody, the recursion ends.
30.5 Example: generating a number series

x: SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i + 1 FROM n WHERE i < 5)

b.x: Without the WHERE i < 5 condition the recursion would never stop. Always give the recursive member a way to run out of rows, or add a LIMIT in the outer query.
30.6 Example: graph reachability with cycle protection
Edges A to B, B to C, C to A and C to D contain a cycle A, B, C, A. We keep the path travelled so far and refuse to visit a node twice.

x: CREATE TABLE edge(a TEXT, b TEXT);
FROM reach r JOIN edge e ON e.a = r.node
WHERE instr(r.path, e.b) = 0)       -- not visited yet
--  D   | ABCD      (C -> A is skipped: A is already in the path)

Forgetting cycle protection on graph data. A cycle makes the recursion infinite and the query runs until the system stops it or runs out of memory. PostgreSQL also offers CYCLE and SEARCH clauses (version 14 and later) that automate this.

b.x: 30.7 Example: bill of materials

x: CREATE TABLE bom(part TEXT, sub TEXT, qty INT);
SELECT b.sub, n.qty * b.qty FROM need n JOIN bom b ON b.part = n.part)
SELECT part, qty FROM need ORDER BY part;

b.x: The quantity multiplies down the tree: one bike needs 2 wheels, and each wheel needs 32 spokes, so 64 spokes in total.
30.8 Performance notes

x: A CTE is not automatically faster than a subquery. Some systems inline it into the main query, others compute it once and store it.
PostgreSQL 12 and later inline a non-recursive CTE that is used once, unless you write AS MATERIALIZED to force a separate computation or AS NOT MATERIALIZED to force inlining.
A recursive CTE should be driven by an indexed join column (here emp.mgr) or each round will scan the whole table.
For very deep hierarchies that are queried often, consider storing a path column or a closure table (see Topic 20).

Name the three parts of a recursive CTE (anchor, recursive member, termination) and give one hierarchy example. Mention that the keyword RECURSIVE is required in SQLite and PostgreSQL, but SQL Server and Oracle omit it.

sec.t: Correlated Subqueries, EXISTS, ANY/ALL and Query Rewriting
sec.s: How correlated subqueries run, EXISTS versus IN, ANY and ALL, and classic exam queries.

b.x: 31.1 Correlated and uncorrelated subqueries

Topic 11 introduced subqueries. An uncorrelated subquery does not mention the outer query and can be evaluated once. A correlated subquery refers to a column of the outer row, so it conceptually runs once for each outer row.

x: -- emp(id, name, mgr, salary, dept) used in this section:
-- 1 Anil  NULL 90000 CSE   | 2 Bina 1 70000 CSE   | 3 Chetan 1 65000 ECE
-- 4 Divya 2    50000 CSE   | 5 Esha 2 50000 CSE   | 6 Farhan 3 45000 ECE
-- employees paid more than the average of THEIR OWN department
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp x WHERE x.dept = e.dept)
ORDER BY name;          -- Anil, Bina, Chetan

b.x: Read it as a loop: for each employee e, compute the average of x.dept = e.dept, then compare. The inner query is different for every outer row because e.dept changes. Optimizers often rewrite such queries into a join with a grouped table, so they are usually faster than this mental loop suggests.
31.2 EXISTS and NOT EXISTS
EXISTS (subquery) is TRUE if the subquery returns at least one row and FALSE otherwise. The columns selected do not matter, so SELECT 1 is the convention. EXISTS stops at the first matching row.

x: SELECT name FROM emp e WHERE EXISTS (
SELECT 1 FROM emp x WHERE x.mgr = e.id);      -- Anil, Bina, Chetan
SELECT name FROM emp e WHERE NOT EXISTS (
SELECT 1 FROM emp x WHERE x.mgr = e.id);      -- Divya, Esha, Farhan

b.x: 31.3 EXISTS versus IN versus JOIN

x: Compares a value with a list. Simple to read. NOT IN is dangerous with NULLs (see below).
Checks for the existence of a matching row. NULL-safe. Good for correlation and for semi-join logic.
Combines columns of both tables. A one-to-many join can repeat the left row, so you may need DISTINCT; EXISTS never repeats it.

NOT IN with a subquery that returns a NULL returns no rows at all. If the list is (1, 2, NULL), then 3 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE. NOT EXISTS has no such trap, so prefer NOT EXISTS for anti-joins.

b.x: 31.4 ANY and ALL

x > ANY (subquery) is true if x is greater than at least one value returned; x > ALL (subquery) is true if x is greater than every value. = ANY is the same as IN. The empty-set cases are a classic trap: x > ALL (empty result) is TRUE, because there is no value that fails, while x > ANY (empty result) is FALSE.

x: SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > ALL (SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 'ECE');
-- SQLite has no ANY / ALL. Rewrite with MAX or MIN:
WHERE salary > (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE dept = 'ECE');
Same as > (SELECT MAX(...)), except when S is empty (ALL gives TRUE, MAX gives NULL so the comparison is not true)

b.x: 31.5 Scalar subqueries and LATERAL

A scalar subquery returns exactly one value and can be used wherever an expression is allowed, for example in the SELECT list. If it returns two rows the statement fails. PostgreSQL, MySQL 8 and Oracle also offer LATERAL, which lets a subquery in FROM refer to columns of tables listed earlier in the same FROM, enabling 'top-N per row' patterns.

x: -- PostgreSQL: the two best-paid employees of each department
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT dept FROM emp) d,
LATERAL (SELECT name, salary FROM emp e
WHERE e.dept = d.dept ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 2) t;

b.x: 31.6 Classic exam queries, several ways
Second highest salary. Salaries in our table are 90000, 70000, 65000, 50000, 50000, 45000, so the answer is 70000.

x: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp);
-- 2. LIMIT / OFFSET (use DISTINCT so duplicates do not count twice)
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;
-- 3. correlated count: exactly one distinct salary is higher
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT salary) FROM emp x WHERE x.salary > e.salary) = 1;

b.x: Highest paid in each department, including ties:

x: SELECT dept, name, salary FROM emp e
WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp x WHERE x.dept = e.dept)
ORDER BY dept;          -- CSE Anil 90000 | ECE Chetan 65000

b.x: Find duplicate values:

x: SELECT salary, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY salary HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

b.x: The n-th highest salary generalises query 3: replace 1 by n - 1. With window functions (Topic 29) the same job is DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) = n.
31.7 Rewriting between forms

x: IN subquery to JOIN: SELECT ... FROM a WHERE a.x IN (SELECT y FROM b) is equal to a join with DISTINCT b.y, or to a semi-join with EXISTS.
NOT IN to NOT EXISTS: do this whenever the subquery column might be NULL.
Correlated scalar subquery to JOIN with GROUP BY: compute the aggregate once per group and join, instead of once per row.
Optimizers do many of these rewrites automatically, but writing the clearest form first and checking the plan (Topic 35) is the right habit.

In a viva you may be asked 'which is faster, IN or EXISTS?'. A good answer: it depends on the optimizer and the data sizes; modern systems treat them similarly, but EXISTS is safer with NULLs and NOT EXISTS is the correct anti-join.

sec.t: Modern SQL: UPSERT, RETURNING, MERGE, JSON, Pagination and Full-Text Search
sec.s: Insert-or-update, returning changed rows, MERGE, JSON columns, efficient paging and text search.

b.x: 32.1 UPSERT: insert or update in one statement

Applications often need 'insert this row, but if the key already exists, update it instead'. Doing a SELECT followed by an INSERT or UPDATE is slow and unsafe under concurrency, because another session can insert between your two statements. UPSERT does it atomically.

x: CREATE TABLE stock(item TEXT PRIMARY KEY, qty INT);
ON CONFLICT(item) DO UPDATE SET qty = qty + excluded.qty;
ON CONFLICT(item) DO UPDATE SET qty = qty + excluded.qty;
SELECT * FROM stock ORDER BY item;     -- ink 3 | pen 15

b.x: The special name excluded refers to the row that was proposed for insertion. MySQL uses INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE with VALUES(col). SQLite also has INSERT OR REPLACE, but be careful: it deletes the old row and inserts a new one, so columns you did not mention return to their defaults and delete triggers or cascading foreign keys fire.
32.2 RETURNING

RETURNING gives back the rows affected by INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE, so you do not need a second SELECT to learn generated keys or final values. It exists in PostgreSQL, SQLite 3.35+ and Oracle (as RETURNING INTO); SQL Server uses the OUTPUT clause.

x: INSERT INTO stock VALUES ('cap', 7) RETURNING item, qty;     -- cap | 7
UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE item = 'pen' RETURNING qty;

b.x: 32.3 MERGE

MERGE is the SQL-standard statement for 'synchronise a target table with a source'. For each source row it can update the matching target row, insert a missing one, or delete. It is available in Oracle, SQL Server, DB2 and PostgreSQL 15 and later. SQLite and older MySQL do not have it; use UPSERT instead.

x: USING incoming s ON t.item = s.item
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET qty = t.qty + s.qty
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (item, qty) VALUES (s.item, s.qty);

b.x: 32.4 JSON in relational databases

Modern relational systems can store JSON text or a binary JSON type and query inside it. This is useful for sparse or evolving attributes, but the core data that you join and filter on still belongs in proper columns.

x: CREATE TABLE ev(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, doc TEXT);
-- PostgreSQL (jsonb column, can be indexed with GIN)
CREATE INDEX ev_gin ON ev USING GIN (doc);
Putting everything in a JSON column to avoid design work. You lose type checking, foreign keys and simple indexing, and queries become hard to optimise. Use JSON for the flexible part only.

b.x: 32.5 Pagination: OFFSET versus keyset

The simple way to show page 2 of results is LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3. The database must still produce and throw away the first 3 rows, so page 10,000 costs far more than page 1. Keyset (seek) pagination remembers the last key seen and asks for rows after it, which an index answers directly.

x: -- OFFSET pagination: reads and discards the skipped rows
SELECT id, msg FROM logs ORDER BY id LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3;      -- 4, 5, 6
-- keyset pagination: last id seen on the previous page was 3
SELECT id, msg FROM logs WHERE id > 3 ORDER BY id LIMIT 3;  -- 4, 5, 6
Both return the same page, but the keyset query uses the index on id and its cost does not grow with the page number.
Keyset pagination needs a unique, ordered key (add a tie-breaker column when sorting by a non-unique column) and cannot jump straight to page 500.
OFFSET results can skip or repeat rows if data changes between page requests; keyset results are more stable.

b.x: 32.6 Full-text search

A query such as WHERE body LIKE '%index%' cannot use a normal B-tree index because of the leading wildcard, so it scans every row, and it does not understand word forms or ranking. Full-text search builds an inverted index that maps each word to the documents containing it, as the index at the back of a book does.

x: CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE notes USING fts5(title, body);
INSERT INTO notes VALUES ('ACID','atomicity consistency isolation durability'),
SELECT title FROM notes WHERE notes MATCH 'index';          -- Index
SELECT title FROM notes WHERE notes MATCH 'hash OR atomicity' ORDER BY rank;
SELECT highlight(notes, 1, '[', ']') FROM notes WHERE notes MATCH 'search';

b.x: PostgreSQL offers tsvector and tsquery with GIN indexes, MySQL has FULLTEXT indexes, and dedicated engines such as Elasticsearch are used when search is the main workload (see Unit 4, Topic 35).

x: Remember three phrases: UPSERT is atomic insert-or-update, RETURNING avoids a second query, and keyset pagination beats OFFSET for deep pages because it seeks through an index instead of skipping rows.

sec.t: DCL and TCL in SQL: GRANT, REVOKE, Roles and Transaction Control
sec.s: Privileges, roles, GRANT OPTION and cascading REVOKE, plus COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT.

b.x: 33.1 Data Control Language

DCL statements decide who may do what. Access control in theory (DAC and RBAC) was covered in Unit 4; this topic shows the SQL that implements it. GRANT gives a privilege and REVOKE takes it back. The statements below work in PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle. SQLite has no users and no GRANT or REVOKE at all, because it is an embedded library whose security is the operating-system permission on the database file.

x: GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON student TO asha;
GRANT UPDATE (cgpa) ON student TO ravi;          -- column-level
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON course TO PUBLIC;       -- every user (use with care)
REVOKE INSERT ON student FROM asha;
-- common privileges: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER,
-- EXECUTE (on functions), USAGE (on schemas and sequences)

b.x: 33.2 WITH GRANT OPTION and cascading revoke

If a privilege is granted WITH GRANT OPTION, the receiver may pass it on to other users. This builds a chain of grants. When the original grantor revokes the privilege, what happens to the people further down the chain? In the standard behaviour (and in PostgreSQL with CASCADE) their privileges are revoked too, unless they also received it from some other source.

x: GRANT SELECT ON student TO dean WITH GRANT OPTION;
-- dean runs:  GRANT SELECT ON student TO hod;
-- hod runs:   GRANT SELECT ON student TO teacher;
REVOKE SELECT ON student FROM dean CASCADE;
-- removes dean's privilege AND the grants dean made (hod, teacher)
REVOKE SELECT ON student FROM dean RESTRICT;
-- fails if dean has passed the privilege on

b.x: 33.3 Roles

A role is a named bundle of privileges. Give privileges to the role once, then add or remove users from the role. This is exactly the RBAC model of Unit 4 expressed in SQL, and it keeps administration manageable when staff change.

x: GRANT SELECT, UPDATE ON marks TO faculty;
GRANT faculty TO meera, rahul;      -- users inherit the privileges
REVOKE faculty FROM rahul;          -- one statement removes all of them

Least privilege: grant only the minimum needed, prefer roles over individual grants, and use views for row or column restriction (a view can expose only some columns, and you grant SELECT on the view, not on the table).

b.x: 33.4 Transaction Control Language

TCL groups SQL statements into transactions (see Unit 3). By default most systems run in autocommit mode, where each statement is its own transaction. Starting a transaction explicitly turns autocommit off until you finish it.

x: Make all changes permanent and visible to others.
Mark a point inside the transaction.
Undo only the work after the savepoint; the transaction stays open.
Forget a savepoint without undoing anything.
CREATE TABLE acct(id INT PRIMARY KEY, bal INT);
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 30 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 999 WHERE id = 2;   -- a mistake
ROLLBACK TO s1;                                  -- undo only the mistake
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 30 WHERE id = 2;

b.x: The transfer of 30 from account 1 to account 2 is atomic: either both updates are saved or neither is. The savepoint let us discard the faulty update without abandoning the whole transaction.
33.5 Transactions in SQLite

SQLite allows many readers or one writer at a time. BEGIN (also called BEGIN DEFERRED) takes no lock until the first read or write. BEGIN IMMEDIATE takes the write lock straight away, so other writers wait and you cannot be surprised later by a 'database is locked' error halfway through. BEGIN EXCLUSIVE additionally blocks readers in the default journal mode. In Python's sqlite3 module you can set isolation_level=None to control BEGIN and COMMIT yourself.

x: BEGIN IMMEDIATE;      -- reserve the write lock now
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 30 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 30 WHERE id = 2;

b.x: 33.6 SET TRANSACTION and isolation

In PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle you choose how strongly a transaction is isolated from others with SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL (READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE). The meaning of each level, the anomalies it allows and the differences between products are explained in Unit 3, Topic 35.

x: -- if the commit fails with SQLSTATE 40001, retry the whole transaction
Assuming DDL can always be rolled back. In PostgreSQL and SQLite CREATE TABLE is transactional, but in MySQL and Oracle most DDL statements commit the current transaction implicitly.

sec.t: Procedural SQL: Functions, Cursors, Exceptions and Advanced Triggers
sec.s: Stored functions versus procedures, cursors, error handling, trigger timing and the mutating-table problem.

b.x: 34.1 Why procedural extensions?

Plain SQL is declarative: you say what you want, not how to compute it. Many tasks, however, need variables, loops, conditions and error handling that run next to the data. Database vendors therefore add a procedural language on top of SQL. Topic 13 introduced stored procedures; here we compare functions and procedures and add cursors, exceptions and triggers in depth.
34.2 Function versus procedure

x: Returns a value (or a table) and can be used inside a SELECT, WHERE or other expression. Normally should not change data, and many systems forbid it inside queries.
Called on its own with CALL or EXEC. May return nothing, has OUT parameters, may modify data and (in most systems) control transactions with COMMIT and ROLLBACK.
A special function the system runs automatically when an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE occurs.

b.x: 34.3 Procedural languages of the main products

x: PL/pgSQL (and PL/Python, PL/Perl and others). Functions are written between dollar quotes: CREATE FUNCTION f() RETURNS ... AS $$ ... $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
Stored routine syntax with DECLARE, BEGIN ... END, DELIMITER commands in the client.
PL/SQL, organised in blocks (DECLARE, BEGIN, EXCEPTION, END) and packages.
T-SQL with BEGIN TRY ... END TRY and BEGIN CATCH.
No stored procedures or functions in SQL. You write functions in the host language (for example Python's create_function) and use triggers for in-database logic.

b.x: 34.4 Cursors

A query returns a set, but a procedural program handles one row at a time. A cursor is a pointer that walks through the result set. Its life cycle has four steps: DECLARE the cursor with its query, OPEN it to run the query, FETCH rows one by one into variables until no row is left, and CLOSE it to release resources.

x: CURSOR c IS SELECT name, salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 'CSE';

b.x: In Python's sqlite3 the cursor is an object you create with connection.cursor(); iterating over it fetches rows lazily, which is the same idea at application level.

x: Using a cursor loop for work that one UPDATE or INSERT ... SELECT can do. Row-by-row processing is often hundreds of times slower than a single set-based statement. Use cursors only when each row really needs separate logic.

b.x: 34.5 Exception handling

Errors such as a constraint violation, a divide by zero or a missing row should be caught inside the routine so that it can clean up or report a clear message. The syntax differs, but the idea is a protected block followed by handlers.
In most systems an exception inside a block undoes the block's own changes (an implicit savepoint) before the handler runs, which keeps the data consistent.
34.6 Triggers in depth
A trigger is code attached to a table that the DBMS runs automatically when a specified event happens. It is defined by its timing, its event, and its level.

x: Runs before the change. Can validate or modify the new values, or cancel the operation.
Runs after the change succeeded. Typical for audit logs and cascading work in other tables.
Replaces the operation. Used on views so that they can be made updatable.
Runs once for each affected row and can read OLD (the row before) and NEW (the row after).
Runs once per statement regardless of how many rows changed. Not available in SQLite and MySQL (they are row-level only).

b.x: OLD exists for UPDATE and DELETE; NEW exists for INSERT and UPDATE. Here is an audit trigger and a guard trigger that run in SQLite and in the DBMS Lab:

x: CREATE TABLE acct(id INT PRIMARY KEY, bal INT);
CREATE TABLE audit(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, what TEXT, old INT, new INT);
CREATE TRIGGER trg_bal AFTER UPDATE OF bal ON acct
CREATE TRIGGER trg_neg BEFORE UPDATE ON acct WHEN NEW.bal < 0
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 10 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE acct SET bal = -5 WHERE id = 1;
-- Error: negative balance      (the update is cancelled)

b.x: 34.7 The mutating-table problem

Oracle raises ORA-04091 'table is mutating' if a row-level trigger tries to query or modify the same table that is being changed by the statement that fired it, because the table is in an inconsistent state halfway through the statement. The usual fixes are to use a statement-level trigger, to collect the changed keys in a temporary structure and process them in an AFTER STATEMENT trigger (a compound trigger), or to rethink the design so that a constraint does the job.
34.8 Trigger pitfalls

x: Hidden logic: someone reading the application code does not see what the trigger does. Document triggers.
Cascades and loops: trigger A updates a table whose trigger B updates the first table again. Systems limit the depth, but design to avoid it.
Performance: a row-level trigger on a bulk load runs once per row and can slow the load massively.
Order: when several triggers fire for the same event, the order may be undefined or may depend on creation order.
Prefer declarative tools (CHECK, FOREIGN KEY, DEFAULT, generated columns) whenever they can express the rule; use triggers only for what they cannot.

Define a trigger with the ECA pattern: Event (INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE), Condition (the WHEN clause) and Action (the body). Give one use case such as an audit log and one danger such as hidden recursion.

sec.s: How a query becomes a plan, heuristic and cost-based optimization, join algorithms with costs, and reading EXPLAIN.

b.x: 35.1 From SQL text to results
SQL says what result you want; the DBMS decides how to get it. A query passes through four phases.

x: Parsing and validation: check the syntax, resolve table and column names with the catalog, check privileges and types.
Rewriting: expand views, simplify expressions, convert the query into relational algebra (a logical plan).
Optimization: choose the cheapest physical plan: which indexes, which join algorithm, which join order.
Execution: run the plan and return rows, usually through a pipeline of iterators that pass rows upwards one at a time.

b.x: A logical plan describes operators (σ selection, π projection, ⋈ join). A physical plan names the algorithms (index scan, hash join, sort). Many physical plans implement the same logical plan with very different costs, and the optimizer's task is to find a cheap one without spending too long searching.
35.2 Heuristic (rule-based) optimization
Some rewrites are almost always beneficial, so optimizers apply them first. They rely on the equivalence rules of relational algebra from Topic 24.

x: Push selections down: apply σ as early as possible so that fewer rows flow into the joins.
Push projections down: drop unneeded columns early so that rows are narrower.
Break conjunctive selections apart: σ(a AND b)(R) = σ(a)(σ(b)(R)), so each part can move to the table it belongs to.
Replace a Cartesian product followed by a selection with a join.
Join the most selective, smallest inputs first.
Query: SELECT name FROM student s JOIN enrol e ON e.roll = s.roll
Naive plan:        π name ( σ course='DBMS' ( student ⋈ enrol ) )
Optimized plan:    π name ( student ⋈ ( σ course='DBMS' (enrol) ) )
-- the selection moves below the join, so the join sees only DBMS enrolments

b.x: 35.3 Cost-based optimization and statistics

Modern optimizers estimate the cost (mainly page I/O plus CPU) of candidate plans using statistics stored in the catalog: number of rows, number of pages, number of distinct values per column, minimum and maximum, and often a histogram of the value distribution. Selectivity is the fraction of rows a predicate keeps.

x: Equality on a column with d distinct values:     selectivity = 1 / d
Range a < v with values uniform in [min, max]:   selectivity = (v - min) / (max - min)
AND of independent predicates:                    multiply selectivities
OR of two predicates:                             s1 + s2 - s1 x s2
student has N = 10,000 rows. dept has d = 50 distinct values. cgpa is uniform between 0 and 10.
combined = 0.02 x 0.2 = 0.004, so about 10,000 x 0.004 = 40 rows
If the real data is skewed (most students are CSE), the estimate is wrong and the optimizer may choose a bad plan. Fresh statistics (ANALYZE) and histograms reduce the error.
Multiplying selectivities assumes the columns are independent. Correlated columns (city and pin code, for example) make the product far too small, and the optimizer underestimates the result size.

b.x: 35.4 Join algorithms and their I/O costs
Let R and S be the two inputs with b_R and b_S pages and n_R, n_S rows, and let M be the number of memory buffer pages available. Costs below count page reads.

x: For each row of R scan all of S. Cost about b_R + n_R x b_S. Terrible for large inputs.
Read R in chunks of M - 2 pages and scan S once per chunk. Cost b_R + ceil(b_R / (M - 2)) x b_S. Put the smaller relation as the outer one.
For each row of R look up the match in an index on S. Cost b_R + n_R x c, where c is the cost of one index lookup (3 to 4 page reads for a B+ tree). Excellent when R is small.
Sort both inputs on the join key, then merge. Cost sort(R) + sort(S) + b_R + b_S; just b_R + b_S if already sorted. Good for range or non-equality joins and when output must be sorted.
Partition both inputs by a hash of the join key, then build and probe in memory. Cost about 3 x (b_R + b_S) when the smaller input's partitions fit in memory. Equality joins only.
b_R = 1000 pages (n_R = 10,000 rows), b_S = 500 pages, M = 52 buffer pages, index lookup cost c = 4.
Tuple nested loop (R outer): 1000 + 1000 x 500 = 501,000 page reads (counting page by page)
Block nested loop, R outer: 1000 + ceil(1000/50) x 500 = 1000 + 20 x 500 = 11,000
Block nested loop, S outer: 500 + ceil(500/50) x 1000 = 500 + 10 x 1000 = 10,500   <- better: smaller relation outside
Hash join: 3 x (1000 + 500) = 4,500   <- cheapest for an equality join on large inputs

b.x: The numbers show why the optimizer does not just pick one favourite algorithm: the best choice depends on sizes, available memory, existing indexes and sort order.
35.5 Join ordering

For three or more tables the join order matters enormously because intermediate results can be huge. With n tables there are many possible orders (for left-deep trees, n factorial). Optimizers use dynamic programming to find the cheapest left-deep order for small n and switch to heuristics or genetic search when there are very many tables. Joining small, selective inputs first keeps the intermediate results small.
35.6 Reading EXPLAIN
EXPLAIN shows the plan the optimizer chose. Learn to read at least the access method, the join order and the estimated against actual rows.

x: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM student WHERE roll = 5;
-- SEARCH student USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM student WHERE city = 'Patna';
-- SCAN student                    (no index on city: full table scan)
CREATE INDEX idx_dept_cgpa ON student(dept, cgpa);
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM student WHERE dept='CSE' AND cgpa>8;
-- SEARCH student USING INDEX idx_dept_cgpa (dept=? AND cgpa>?)
-- PostgreSQL: EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and shows real times
-- Seq Scan = full scan | Index Scan / Index Only Scan | Nested Loop,
-- Hash Join, Merge Join | rows= estimate vs actual rows
SCAN means every row is read; SEARCH means an index or the primary key is used. In PostgreSQL, a large gap between estimated and actual rows is a sign of stale statistics or correlated columns.

b.x: 35.7 Writing queries the optimizer can help with
A predicate is SARGable (Search ARGument able) if the database can use an index to evaluate it. Common mistakes make good indexes useless.

x: WHERE UPPER(name) = 'ASHA' cannot use an index on name. Use an expression index, or compare in a form that leaves the column bare.
LIKE '%sha' cannot use a B-tree index; LIKE 'As%' can.
WHERE cgpa * 10 > 80 scans; WHERE cgpa > 8 can use the index.
Comparing a text column with a number can force a conversion of every row.
Prevents covering-index plans and moves unneeded data.
An index on (dept, cgpa) does not help a query on cgpa alone.
The application runs one query for a list and then one per row. Replace with one join or one IN query.

A complete answer to 'how does the optimizer work' mentions: logical to physical plan, heuristic rules (push selection down), cost estimates from statistics, join algorithm and join order choices, and the use of indexes.

sec.t: SQL Injection in Depth: Attack Types and Layered Defenses
sec.s: How the main kinds of SQL injection work, why some defences fail, and a layered defence you can implement.

b.x: 36.1 Recap and purpose

Topics 15 to 18 explained the threat and showed parameterised queries. This topic classifies the attacks so that you can recognise them, and explains why a defence must be layered. The examples are minimal and for learning how to defend your own systems; testing any system you do not own or have permission for is illegal.
36.2 The root cause in one picture

SQL injection happens when user input is concatenated into the SQL text, so the database cannot tell data from code. The same Python function can be unsafe or safe depending only on how the statement is built.

x: db.executescript("CREATE TABLE users(id INT, name TEXT, pw TEXT);"
def unsafe(name):      # BAD: input becomes part of the SQL text
return db.execute("SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE name='%s'" % name).fetchall()
def safe(name):        # GOOD: input is bound as a value
return db.execute("SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE name=?", (name,)).fetchall()
safe(attack)     # []                            <- treated as a strange name

b.x: 36.3 Types of SQL injection

x: The attacker makes the query fail and reads details from the error message (table names, column names, versions). Fix: never show raw database errors to users.
The attacker appends UNION SELECT ... so that data from another table appears in the normal page. It needs the same number of columns and compatible types, which attackers discover by trial.
The page shows no data, but it behaves differently when a condition is true or false. The attacker asks many yes/no questions to extract data one bit at a time.
The attacker injects a delay that runs only when a condition is true and measures the response time. Works even when the page looks identical.
The database is made to send data to a server the attacker controls (for example by a DNS or HTTP request from a database function). Needs particular database features.

Malicious input is stored safely at first (for example as a username) and later used unsafely in a different query, possibly by an administrator tool. Input that was 'sanitised' on entry can still be dangerous at use.

b.x: A UNION-based attack against the unsafe function above looks like this:

x: attack2 = "x' UNION SELECT id, pw FROM users--"

b.x: The quote closes the string, UNION adds a second query, and -- comments out the rest of the original statement.
36.4 Why 'we use an ORM' or 'we use stored procedures' is not enough

x: ORMs generate parameterised queries for normal operations, but every ORM has a raw SQL escape hatch. Building strings there reintroduces the problem.
A stored procedure that builds dynamic SQL inside itself with concatenation (EXECUTE IMMEDIATE, sp_executesql or EXECUTE with a string) is as injectable as application code.
Parameters protect values only. Table names, column names and sort directions cannot be bound as parameters.

b.x: 36.5 Identifiers: allow-listing
When the user chooses a sort column ('ORDER BY'), a table or a direction, check it against a fixed list in your code and place only the list's own constants into the SQL.

x: return db.execute(f'SELECT * FROM student ORDER BY {col} {d}')

b.x: 36.6 The layered defence

x: Parameterised queries or prepared statements for every value. This is the primary and most effective control.
Allow-list validation for identifiers, and sensible validation of types, lengths and formats for inputs (a secondary control, never the only one).

Least privilege: the web application's database account should have only the table privileges it needs, no DROP, no access to system tables, no file or OS functions, and separate accounts for read-only pages.
Hide internals: generic error messages to users, detailed errors only in server logs.
Avoid dynamic SQL in stored procedures, or build it with proper quoting functions and bound parameters.

Monitoring and WAF: a web application firewall and database activity monitoring catch known attack patterns and give alerts. They reduce risk but are a safety net, not a fix; clever encodings can bypass them.
Test and review: static analysis, code review of every raw query, and authorised security testing (for example scanning your own application in a test environment).

Trying to defend by removing or escaping quote characters yourself. Hand-written escaping misses encodings, numeric contexts (no quotes needed in WHERE id = 5 OR 1=1) and second-order cases. Use parameters.

In answers, give the cause (data mixed with code), one example attack with its effect, the primary defence (parameterised queries) and at least two supporting controls (least privilege and error handling).

sec.s: Fifteen answered questions and five self-check exercises on topics 24 to 36.

b.x: 39.1 Questions with answers

x: 1. Explain the division operator and write its SQL equivalent.

R ÷ S returns the values of the attributes of R that are not in S for which R contains a row paired with every row of S. Example: students who took all courses. SQL has no division, so it is written with a double NOT EXISTS (no course exists that the student has not taken) or with GROUP BY and HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT course) equal to the total number of courses.
2. Differentiate tuple relational calculus and domain relational calculus.

Tuple calculus uses variables that range over tuples of relations, as in { t | Student(t) AND t.cgpa > 8 }. Domain calculus uses variables that range over attribute values, as in { <n, c> | Student(n, c) AND c > 8 }. Both are declarative and, for safe expressions, equivalent in power to relational algebra (Codd's theorem).
3. What is a safe expression in relational calculus?

An expression that is guaranteed to produce a finite result that uses only values from the database. { t | NOT Student(t) } is unsafe because infinitely many tuples are not in Student. Safety is needed so that queries can actually be evaluated.
4. Why does NOT IN return no rows when the subquery contains a NULL?

x NOT IN (a, b, NULL) is x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> NULL. The last comparison is UNKNOWN, so the whole condition can never be TRUE. NOT EXISTS avoids the problem because it checks only whether a matching row exists.
5. When would you choose LEFT JOIN instead of INNER JOIN?

Use LEFT JOIN when rows of the left table must appear even without a match, for example listing all students with the number of courses taken, including students with zero. An inner join would drop those students. Remember that a filter on the right table in WHERE turns the outer join back into an inner join; put it in ON instead.
6. What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
UNION removes duplicate rows from the combined result, which requires sorting or hashing. UNION ALL keeps every row and is faster. Use UNION ALL when duplicates are impossible or harmless.
7. Explain COALESCE and NULLIF with examples.

COALESCE(a, b, c) returns the first non-NULL argument, for example COALESCE(phone, 'none'). NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a equals b and a otherwise, which is useful to avoid division by zero: total / NULLIF(count, 0).
WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and cannot use aggregate functions. HAVING filters groups after aggregation and can use aggregates such as COUNT(*) > 5. A query can have both.
9. How does a window function differ from GROUP BY?

GROUP BY collapses rows into one row per group. A window function computes an aggregate or rank over a set of related rows but keeps every input row, so you can show each student's score next to the department average or rank.
10. What are the parts of a recursive CTE and how does it terminate?

An anchor member supplies the starting rows, a recursive member joins the CTE to a table to produce the next level, and the members are combined with UNION ALL. The recursion ends when the recursive member returns no new rows; cycles must be prevented by tracking visited nodes or a depth limit.
11. What is a correlated subquery and when is it executed?

A correlated subquery refers to a column of the outer query, so its result depends on the current outer row. Conceptually it is evaluated once per outer row, although optimizers often turn it into a join.
12. Explain UPSERT and why it is better than SELECT followed by INSERT or UPDATE.

UPSERT (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, or MERGE) inserts a row or updates the existing one in a single atomic statement. A separate SELECT-then-write sequence has a race window in which another session can insert the same key, causing duplicate errors or lost updates.
13. Compare block nested-loop join and hash join.

Block nested loop reads the outer relation in memory-sized blocks and scans the inner relation once per block: b_R + ceil(b_R/(M-2)) x b_S page reads. Hash join partitions both inputs by a hash of the join key and joins matching partitions, costing about 3(b_R + b_S) if partitions fit in memory. Hash join is much cheaper for large equality joins but cannot handle range joins.
14. What makes a predicate SARGable? Give two examples that are not.

A SARGable predicate can use an index because the indexed column appears alone on one side of the comparison. WHERE UPPER(name) = 'ASHA' and WHERE cgpa * 10 > 80 are not SARGable because they apply an expression to the column. LIKE '%sha' is not either because of the leading wildcard.
15. List four defences against SQL injection in order of importance.

First, parameterised queries or prepared statements. Second, allow-listing of identifiers and input validation. Third, least-privilege database accounts. Fourth, hiding database errors, with monitoring and a WAF as extra layers. Escaping by hand is not a reliable defence.

sec.s: Final checklist and glossary for the extended Unit 2 topics.

b.x: Division (÷)
Relational algebra operator for 'for all' queries; written in SQL with double NOT EXISTS or GROUP BY and HAVING.
Relational calculus
Declarative query languages (tuple and domain) based on predicate logic; safe expressions are equivalent to relational algebra.
Anti-join and semi-join
Rows of A without (NOT EXISTS) or with (EXISTS) a match in B.
Three-valued logic
TRUE, FALSE and UNKNOWN; comparisons with NULL give UNKNOWN.
Window function
A function computed over a window of related rows (OVER clause) without collapsing the rows.
CTE
A named temporary result introduced by WITH; recursive CTEs have an anchor and a recursive member.
Correlated subquery
A subquery that references the outer row.
UPSERT
Atomic insert-or-update.
Keyset pagination
Paging by remembering the last key seen instead of skipping rows with OFFSET.
DCL and TCL
GRANT and REVOKE manage privileges; COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT manage transactions.
Cursor
A pointer used to process a query result row by row inside procedural code.
Trigger (ECA)
Event-Condition-Action code run automatically on INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE.
Selectivity
The fraction of rows that satisfy a predicate; used to estimate plan costs.
Join algorithms
Nested loop, block nested loop, index nested loop, sort-merge and hash join.
SARGable
A predicate that can use an index.
SQL injection
Attack in which input changes the structure of a SQL statement; prevented mainly by parameterised queries.
